title: Janus MgAlB_2 MBene: a dipole-engineered anode for ultrafast Li-ion transport and exceptional lithium storage
authors: Pritam Samanta, Sashank Kumar Pandey, Amit Kumar Jana, Prakash Parida
abstract: In this work, we propose a group II/IIIA-based Janus MBene, MgAlB_2, and investigate its electrochemical properties using first-principles calculations. The substitution of one Mg layer in Mg_2B_2 MBene by an Al layer breaks the structural symmetry and generates a permanent out-of-plane polarization, giving rise to a distinct electronic environment compared with the parent Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers. Electronic-structure analysis reveals enhanced orbital hybridization among B, Mg, and Al states near the Fermi level, resulting in improved electronic delocalization across the monolayer. The Janus MgAlB_2 monolayer is found to possess excellent dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability. Owing to its polarization-modified energy landscape, Li ions migrate with an exceptionally low diffusion barrier of 17.1 meV, corresponding to a room-temperature diffusion coefficient of 3.43x10^-10 cm^2/s. Unlike the pristine Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers, which support only a single stable adsorption layer, MgAlB_2 accommodates two complete Li layers. Detailed analysis shows that the residual polarization retained after first-layer lithiation continues to promote Li adsorption, whereas increasing Li-Li electrostatic interactions eventually limit further storage. As a result, the Janus monolayer delivers a high theoretical specific capacity of 1470.24 mAh/g together with a small volume expansion of only 3.7% during maximum lithiation. The present study demonstrates that intrinsic polarization can be utilized to regulate both the thermodynamics and kinetics of Li storage, providing a design strategy for high-rate and high-capacity two-dimensional electrode materials.
summary: This work proposes a novel Janus material, $	ext{MgAlB}_2$, as an advanced anode for Li-ion batteries. By breaking structural symmetry, the material generates an intrinsic polarization that significantly enhances lithium ion transport and storage capacity. The calculations demonstrate this leads to ultra-low diffusion barriers and high theoretical energy density.
main_problem: The research addresses the need for novel, high-performance anode materials for Li-ion batteries that overcome limitations in conventional anodes like graphite.
main_result: The engineered Janus $	ext{MgAlB}_2$ monolayer exhibits exceptional performance, achieving a theoretical specific capacity of $1470.24 	ext{ mAhg}^{-1}$ with an ultralow Li diffusion barrier of $17.1 	ext{ meV}$.
method: The study relies heavily on first-principles calculations (DFT) to model the electronic structure, electrochemical properties, and ion transport kinetics.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 2D Janus material, $	ext{MgAlB}_2$, created by breaking the symmetry of parent $	ext{MBenes}$ ($	ext{Mg}_2	ext{B}_2$ or $	ext{Al}_2	ext{B}_2$) to induce an intrinsic electric polarization.
key_observables: Li migration barrier ($17.1 	ext{ meV}$), theoretical specific capacity ($1470.24 	ext{ mAhg}^{-1}$), out-of-plane dipole moment, and electronic delocalization across the monolayer.
important_parameters: Low diffusion barrier ($	ext{meV}$ scale); room-temperature diffusion coefficient ($3.43	imes 10^{-10} 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{s}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that engineering intrinsic polarization via Janus asymmetry can fundamentally improve both the thermodynamics (capacity) and kinetics (diffusion) of Li storage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate optimized geometries, electrostatic potential maps showing asymmetry, electron localization function (ELF) plots detailing charge transfer upon Li adsorption, and energy profiles mapping the low-barrier diffusion pathway for Li ions.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the structural modification ($	ext{Mg}_2	ext{B}_2 	o 	ext{Janus } 	ext{MgAlB}_2$), analyzing the resulting polarization, and then using computational methods to quantify enhanced electronic delocalization and superior Li-ion transport properties compared to symmetric counterparts.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electrochemistry, the concept of engineering intrinsic dipole moments via structural asymmetry to control charge transport barriers is analogous to designing quantum interfaces or controlling local electric fields in nanoscale devices relevant to AMO physics.
